There are several things they can do. I can think of a few more, but not directly related to the processor.

1) CPU Instruction Set

At the most basic level all conventional processors ultimately operate with very small, direct commands, called instructions. Programming languages are translated into these instructions so that the computer can use them. CPU architectures generally have the same instructions, with later processors adding new instructions. So, for instance, the 80286 had the instructions of the 8086, its predecessor.

However, in some cases, instructions can be REMOVED as well. This is not very common and usually only used with uncommon instructions that were actively causing a problem. So let's say that there's a particular instruction that Windows 7 needs, but is deliberately stricken from these new CPUs. The result is that Windows would likely crash whenever that particular instruction was fed to the processor.

HOWEVER, this is unlikely for many reasons. First, Microsoft would have to convince at least Intel to go along with it. Intel is not terribly likely to agree to it, because one of the reasons they're the king of PC chips is the fact that they are FANTASTIC with backwards compatibility. AMD likely also wouldn't play ball. Keep in mind that these companies are concerned about the rise of mobile electronics as well, where they are not so dominant. Some may say they can't afford not to force their dominance, but others would point out that, with alternatives in the form of said mobile electronics, especially as they move in the direction of desktop substitutes (at least in the case of Android), they can't afford to make their systems deliberately and overly draconian, since customers already have a choice.

Plus, it would clobber any other program that relied on that particular instruction, and it would almost certainly be figured out in fairly short order, so it is unlikely they could "get away" with it very easily.

There are other tricks they could theoretically play in this department, such as fooling around with the rewritable portions of the processor's microcode (small instructions that program parts of the processor very directly), but that strikes me as extremely unlikely, and would likely require, say, installing a poisoned update, which I mention later.

2) Activation

Windows since XP needs to be activated, e.g. registered with Microsoft's servers in a vain attempt to prevent pirated copies from proliferating. This failed most spectacularly, surprising absolutely no one, but it remains. During the activation process, certain information is sent about your computer. It is possible that the activation process would reject any attempt to activate Windows on one of these chips.

This would probably cause some bad legal problems in one way or another, however, so it isn't overly likely. It would also not deter techies who know how to break the Windows activation system (e.g. through cracks, which aren't generally hard to find and use). That said, that's only for consumers - businesses are their target here, and a lot of businesses won't touch pirated software with a ten foot pole for both legal and practical reasons, practical being "the company won't support it."

But, some businesses might still resist. That leads to...

3) Refusal of Support

This is the most likely option, and probably the easiest from a technical standpoint. Sizable companies usually pay big bucks for Microsoft to supply them with software, usually in a way that lets them have some level of flexibility in terms of how they're using it. They also provide resources to these companies. They could simply amend their support procedures so that all of the newer processors are not considered to be "supported," and as such will offer no assistance with them. This can be a big deal, depending on the situation.

This move may be very effective. However, given a lot of other factors in play, it may also backfire spectacularly. Microsoft has been explicitly afraid of pissing off business too much, and this is a blatantly obvious play to force their hand, even though said businesses are less than enthused about Windows 10. In some cases, Windows 10 is outright ILLEGAL to install in its current form, because the spyware portions violate laws and confidentiality agreements.

Finally, we have...

4) Poison updates

There are a very large number of people who think that the instant that they no longer install updates, the correct procedure is to set fire to any disk containing the non-updated operating system and do their best to scourge it from existence forevermore. Yes, this is an exaggeration, but it's not much of one. However, it's entirely possible that new installations will choke down the tons of updates that Windows 7 has. One of these updates could detect the processor and break Windows if it's one they don't want you running. This isn't so easy to pull off for large companies that have their own internal update procedures, but smaller businesses may get smacked with this.

Now, it is important to note that while some of these may be legal, Microsoft might not give a shit. They're going after businesses now. This is huge. Something very rotten is up in Microsoft-ville here, and it's possible they're willing to take a billion dollar lawsuit straight through the face, because if they dig in deep enough they think they can crush any competition, turning the litigation costs into what amounts to an investment. You're not going to be able to dig up what will be then-outdated software and give it a chance on the market since all the customers are locked in to Windows 10.

The biggest thing to note here is that Microsoft will do everything in its power to FORCE you to move all your computing to Windows 10. They have been blatantly opaque about everything regarding Windows 10, despite the fact that much has been found out about its behaviors (e.g. spyware activities) and we have every reason to believe Microsoft will act against the interests of the consumer in any situation they deem it beneficial, and will put that data at risk if it deems it beneficial to them. They also have no problem with doing generally anti-consumer tactics and resorting to deception (recent Windows 10 update notices) and reconfiguring consumer computers as they see fit (turning the 'privacy' options off to restore full spying capabilities). The question is, of course, WHY they are doing it. I suspect something very rotten is going on somewhere. Some say the NSA, but I am inclined to believe that the motivation is business-oriented. I think Microsoft is in trouble in some critical way. They are NOT fucking around here, so that means they've got a lot to lose. It is also possible, however, that they're making up for playing nice for the last decade and a half after the lawsuit, in which case they would have tried to pull this shit with earlier versions of Windows anyway. I think we can expect to see more of this in the future.

Also, obligatory note, as someone is going to say "only Microsoft gets shit on for the privacy violation" - no, they don't, and even if it was only Microsoft it wouldn't make the fact that others do it any better; in fact it just makes Microsoft's attempt WORSE. Furthermore, anyone who says the spyware is backported to Windows 7, IIRC that's only if you joined their "Customer Experience" program, and furthermore, that's only if you accept updates, and yes it is possible to run a secure system without choking down every update Microsoft wants you to trust them on.

IMPORTANT NOTE: There are some other things that they could do to cause problems. One is to muck around with the BIOS/firmware, etc. However, these would all have their own consequences. Nevertheless, they may very well work. That said, this response was keeping an eye firmly on the idea of "supporting the processor," not "anything Microsoft could do to attain lock-in."

ANOTHER IMPORTANT NOTE: We are not going to know precisely what these chips can or cannot do physically until someone actually runs Windows 7 on them. Microsoft can blow all the hot air it wants in that regard, it will do no good if you can load up and run Windows 7 just fine. They can do things like poison updates and refuse support contracts, but they can't really change the laws of physics to break the chip with a press release - although, knowing Microsoft, they're probably working on that.

I have been challenged by /u/MrBlueSky to spend yet more hours of my time researching velomobiles and crunching numbers. I couldn't think of a better way to spend my time. I'd like to make it clear I intend to give cars every handicap I can. If I do this right, your mind will still be blown.

Americans get about 69% of their energy from fossil fuels. Oil makes up only 1% of the energy produced in the US[[1](http://www.afdc.energy.gov/vehicles/electric_emissions.php)] Let's bump that up to 100% to make the comparison easy. To make 1 kWh (Kilowatt-hour) of electricity from oil you need to release 1.67 lbs of CO2.[[2](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.cfm?id=74&t=11)] According to the numbers from [this](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JsqQiBa39-U) rider, it takes around 5.8 Wh to travel a mile in real world conditions.

So now that we know how much CO2 our fuel puts out, we can start calculating how much it takes to actually make and run a Velomobile. So our standard Velomobile is composed mostly of Aluminum. Of course there's rubber for the wheels and some glass for the windscreen, but they're not the main materials here. To make aluminum from raw ore, you need to mine it, transport it, heat it, then separate it from the other material in the rock with an electric current. That last part in particular takes 15 kWh[[3]( http://wordpress.mrreid.org/2011/07/15/electricity-consumption-in-the-production-of-aluminium/)] and releasing 10.91 kg of CO2 per kg of aluminum . This is inefficient. What we can do instead is use recycled aluminum to make the vehicles. As I posted before, it takes 1/20th the energy to recycle a kg of Aluminum, leaving us at an efficient .75 kWh per kg. This comes in as an incredible $2.97 just to process the aluminum for a single velo. What's more since it takes so little power and makes so little pollution, all this can be done in the same country at a fraction of the cost.

Okay, so the things are heavy. It's hard enough to go uphill with a bicycle. You can't reasonably pedal that beast up anything more than a gentle incline. You need a motor to help. Let's go with a simple 250w motor. We're going to need a battery for that motor. MrBlueSky already did me the favor of picking out what battery I'd be using for this one. Lithium Iron Phosphate.[[4](http://www.powerstream.com/LLLF-48v.htm)] 1 kWh should do for this. But how much energy does it take to actually make a Lithium Ion battery? This paper put out by Japan's Central Research Institute of Electric Power Industry suggests it takes a whopping 476.5 kWh and 346.55 kg of CO2 just to make the battery we're looking for.[[5](http://www.electrochem.org/dl/ma/202/pdfs/0068.PDF)] It's not looking good so far.

So why am I ignoring the car? This is Velos vs. Cars 2.0, right? We'll get to them. First I thought I'd set the stage for the most important part of the post: Performance.

The average car in 2015 got 25.3 MPG.[[6](http://www.umich.edu/~umtriswt/EDI_sales-weighted-mpg.html)] A Velomobile can get 175 MPkWh. But how do we meaningfully compare the velo to a car? Aren't these totally different sources of power? That's true. And now you can see why I decided to use oil as our preferred method of power generation. A gallon of oil makes 13.6 kWh.p[[7](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.cfm?id=667&t=6)] It also contains 138,095 Btu over Gasoline's 120,476.[[8](http://www.eia.gov/Energyexplained/?page=about_energy_units)] That's about 12.76% more energy. So tell you what, let's give the average car a nice mileage boost to cover the difference. Now it gets 28.53 MPG.

I don't need to do the math past this point, do I? I'll do it anyways for fun: 175 x 13.6 = 2,380 MPG. I think we've got a winner here. But really, what good is this if you hemorrhage money paying for the expensive battery? What are the savings over just the life of a single battery? Well Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries get up to 2,000 charge/discharge cycles in the lab.[[4](http://www.powerstream.com/LLLF-48v.htm)] That's a maximum of 350,000 miles before your battery needs to be replaced. Since we picked a nice, neat 1 kWh battery we know we've just used up a total of 2,000 kWh for this distance. To get the amount of oil that took, we just divide by 13.6 and get a grand total of 147.06 gallons. Even if we include all the energy it took to melt the aluminum and make the battery, that's still just 183.92 gallons worth of energy from start to finish. If you were the average 35-55 year old male (The most avid drivers, clocking in at 18,858 miles a year)[[9](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/ohim/onh00/bar8.htm)], this battery would last you 18 years, 6 months, and approximately 20 days.

Okay, so what about the car? Okay, so 350,000 / 28.53 = 12,267.79 gallons. That's **just** the car with its efficiency artificially boosted for argument's sake. Never mind that cars need to be shipped around the world and frequently get lower numbers than their ratings, and never mind that velomobiles need less power since you'll be pedaling and don't need as much energy to maintain speed. If you think my analysis is incomplete, I challenge you to name any number of factors that could even hope to bridge this gap.

Fun facts:

1. A gallon of oil makes 19.55 lbs of Carbon Dioxide. [[10](http://www3.epa.gov/otaq/climate/documents/420f14040a.pdf)]

2. 1 kg is almost exactly 2.2 lbs.

3. The two facts before this one let you calculate the environmental impact of the vehicles.

4. Even if the battery didn't last half as long, you'd still only be paying about $200 a year for it. With the cost going down to almost $150 afterwards since you don't have to buy the electrical systems for it.

5. At a cost of $2 per gallon, it would cost you $.07 to travel 1 mile on a car of comparable efficiency to the one used here. At a cost of $.12 per kWh. you'd need to travel 100 miles to spend that same 7 cents on a velo.
